# The provenance file on Sbk

*Provenance record 493 · Sbk · one temple, fully accounted for.*

## Provenance

**1. The attestation.** **𓃣**, from the tradition's own record. On record: Papyrus Westcar (the wax crocodile episode), Herodotus, Histories 2.68–69 (the crocodile and Crocodilopolis), Strabo, Geography 17.1.38 (Petsuchos), Sobek hymns of Medinet Madi (Fayum temple liturgy).

**2. The narrative record.** **The Crocodile Who Emerges from Nun** — The Sobek theology of the Fayum — best preserved in the hymn cycles of the crocodile temples — casts him as the one who first climbed from the primeval waters, creator of the world’s order and of the Nile itself.  Later tradition even made him a form of the sun god’s power, the fierce Eye of Ra returned from the Nubian desert. **The Double Temple** — At Kom Ombo south of Luxor, Sobek shares a perfectly symmetrical double temple with Horus the Elder: one half for the falcon of the sky, one for the crocodile of the river.  The division stages the Egyptian ideal of the Two Lands’ balance — sky and water, kingship and fertility — under one roof.

**3. The physical record.** Crocodilopolis (Shedet, modern Medinet el-Fayum) held the main temple; Kom Ombo’s double temple survives in superb relief, its columns carrying intact crocodile capitals. Crocodile cemeteries at Tebtunis and el-Shams el-Qawassim held mummified sacred crocodiles by the hundreds, each an embodied Sobek buried with honours.

**4. The current holding.** The temple at [/sobek/](/sobek/), a temple of the restored name. aSCII-equivalent form

**5. The documented resonances.** **Agriculture, Food & Harvest**, **Maritime, Shipping & Ocean Industries**, **Pet Care & Animal Industries** — seats argued and weighted in the [pattern atlas](/patterns/), read through the myths in this temple's [Resonance File](/sobek/blog/resonance/).

**6. The primary sources.** [The Book of the Dead](/texts/book-of-the-dead/) — the library this file answers to, open at the [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/).

**7. The continuing record.** The name Sobek survives in the modern scholarly vocabulary of the Nile and appears throughout Egyptological literature as the archetype of Egyptian theriolatry — the worship of a dangerous animal not despite but because of its power.  The Fayum’s temple of Medinet Madi preserves the longest surviving sacred hymn cycles addressed to a crocodile.
